_title: Chain Lab — see how a blockchain works
_desc: Interactive lab: see how a blockchain works — hashes, blocks, mining, tokens. English and Russian.
lede: Every block is a few lines of data and one fingerprint. Change a single letter and the fingerprint breaks. Try it below, right in your browser.
mode1d: Type any text, watch its SHA-256 hash change, then search for a nonce that makes the block valid.
mode2d: Paste a Bitcoin or Ethereum transaction ID and see who sent what, the fee, and which block holds it.
labSub: A block counts as valid when its hash starts with enough zeros. The only way to get there is to try nonce after nonce. That search is what miners do.
seedWarn: This looks like a seed phrase. Never type a real seed phrase into any website, including this one. Anyone who has it owns your wallet.
diffNote: Each extra zero makes the search about 16 times longer. Bitcoin today needs around 19 of them.
found: Found nonce {n} after {t} tries. The block is valid.
stopped: Stopped. Press Mine to continue from this nonce.
timeout: Stopped after 20 seconds to spare your battery. Try a lower difficulty.
edited: You changed the block, so its hash changed. Mine again to make it valid.
learnSub: Four ideas carry the whole technology. Each one has a hands-on step in the course.
l1d: A fixed-length fingerprint of any data. Same input, same hash. One changed letter, a completely different hash.
l2d: Each block stores the hash of the one before it. Edit an old block and every block after it breaks.
l3d: Thousands of computers keep copies and agree on one history without trusting each other.
l4d: Coins, points and unique items like NFTs are entries in a smart contract that anyone can check.
courseSub: Steps 1–5 are open. Steps 6–8 are in progress.
c2d: Data, nonce and the previous hash
c3d: Edit an old block and watch the chain turn red
c4d: Proof of Work, step by step
c5d: Five copies vote out a fake
c6d: Private key, public key, address, signature
c8d: Claim a unique word that only you own
f1: Chain Lab is an educational project. Nothing here is financial advice.
f2: The lab runs fully in your browser. It never asks for a wallet, keys or a seed phrase.
s1x: SHA-256 turns any text into 64 hex characters. Type below, then change just one letter and count how much of the hash changes.
s1diff: {n} of 64 characters changed. A tiny edit gives a completely new fingerprint.
s2t: Block: data plus a link to the past
s2x: A block holds four things: its number, the data, a nonce and the hash of the previous block. All four go into the block's own hash. Edit a field and watch the hash.
eNonce: The number miners change to find a valid hash.
ePrev: Hash of the previous block. This field links blocks into a chain.
eHash: Computed from the four fields above. You can't type it, only change the inputs.
s3t: Chain: why the past can't be edited
s3x: These four blocks are already mined with 3 zeros. Change the data in block 2. Its hash changes, block 3 now points to a hash that no longer exists, and the damage runs to the end. To fake history you would have to re-mine every block after the edit.
chainBroken: The chain is broken from block #{k}. Mine the red blocks from left to right to repair it.
s4x: There is no shortcut to a hash with N zeros, only guessing. Each extra zero multiplies the work by about 16. Run the race to mine with 1 to 4 zeros.
raceDone: Each row took roughly 16 times more guesses than the one above. Your numbers vary because guessing is random. That cost is what protects the chain.
s4n: Real networks make quintillions of guesses per second. Ethereum stopped mining in 2022 and moved to Proof of Stake, where validators lock up coins instead of burning electricity.
s5x: Three computers keep the same chain. Edit a block on any one of them. That copy no longer matches the others, so the network ignores it. Even if you re-mine it, two honest copies still outvote you.
s5n: Try it: change the same block to the same text on two nodes and re-mine both. Now the fake has the majority. That is a 51% attack, and on a real network it needs more than half of all computing power.
courseSub2: All 8 steps are open. Start anywhere.
s6t: Keys: proving it's you without a password
s6x: A wallet is a pair of keys. The private key signs, the public key lets anyone check the signature, and the address is a short hash of the public key. Sign a message, then try to change it in the check field.
privWarn: Whoever has the private key owns the wallet. Real wallets never show it to websites.
sigBad: Invalid. The message or signature doesn't match this key.
s6n: Simplified: Bitcoin and Ethereum use the secp256k1 curve, and Ethereum builds addresses with Keccak-256. This lab uses P-256 and SHA-256, which are built into your browser. The idea is the same.
s7t: Transactions: a wallet holds keys, not coins
s7x: Your balance isn't stored anywhere. It's the sum of every transaction in the chain. A transaction is a signed message: who pays whom and how much. Miners collect them into a block and check each one.
sentOk: Signature checks out. The transaction is waiting for a block.
sentForged: Rejected at once: signed by {s}, but the coins belong to {f}.
noTx: Nothing to mine: send a transaction first.
s7n: Try a double spend: Alice has 10. Send 8 from Alice to Bob, then 8 from Alice to Carol, then mine. Only the first one gets in.
s8x: A token is a record in a smart contract. Coins like USDT are fungible (ERC-20): any one is as good as another. NFTs (ERC-721) are unique: each has its own ID and exactly one owner. This contract is a name registry. The token ID is the hash of the word, so the same word can't be minted twice.
taken: "{w}" already belongs to {o}. There is only one original.
mixed: Rejected: Latin and Cyrillic letters are mixed. This is a classic fake, a lookalike word (homoglyph).
badWord: Use 3–20 letters, digits or hyphens, in one alphabet.
transferNote: Only the current owner can sign a transfer. Changing the owner here is that owner's signed transfer.
s8n: Uniqueness lives inside one contract. Anyone can deploy another contract with the same word, and people trust the original because of its address. ENS names (.eth) work exactly like this.
decodeSub: Paste a transaction ID from Bitcoin or Ethereum. The data comes from the real network through a public API. No wallet, no keys.
badFormat: This isn't a transaction ID. Bitcoin uses 64 hex characters, like {btc}. Ethereum uses 0x plus 64 hex characters, like {eth}.
netError: Couldn't reach the server. Check your connection and try again.
eTxHash: The transaction's own hash: its fingerprint, like the block hashes in the course.
eStatus: Confirmed means a block holds it. In the mempool means it is signed and sent, but no block holds it yet.
eStatusFailed: Included in a block, but the contract call reverted. The fee was still paid.
eBlock: The block that holds the transaction and when it was made.
eConf: Blocks built on top, counting its own. Each one makes rewriting it harder.
eInputs: Earlier outputs this transaction spends. Each is spent whole, like a banknote.
eOutputs: New amounts locked to addresses. What the sender keeps comes back as change.
eFeeBtc: Inputs minus outputs. The miner who made the block keeps it.
eSize: Space taken in the block. Bitcoin fees are priced per virtual byte (vB).
eFromEth: The account that signed the transaction.
eToEth: The account or contract that receives it.
eFeeEth: Gas used × gas price. Paid even if the transaction fails.
eGas: Gas measures computation. A plain ETH transfer uses 21,000.
utxoNote: How Bitcoin counts: there are no balances, only unspent outputs (UTXO). A transaction takes whole earlier outputs as inputs and creates new outputs. If the inputs hold more than the payment, the extra comes back to the sender as a change output. Whatever is left between inputs and outputs is the fee.
noChangeNote: This one has no change: the inputs add up to exactly the payment plus the fee.
gasNote: How Ethereum counts: accounts have balances, like a bank. Every step of computation costs gas. The sender sets a gas limit and a price, pays gas used × price, and unused gas is not charged.
contractNote: This transaction calls a smart contract. Token transfers happen inside the contract and are not shown here, so the ETH amount can be 0.
